articles.title: Russian Nuclear Ballistic Missile Submarines Are Now Cocooned In Nets
articles.text:
From recent satellite imagery, the Russian Navy now looks to be using nets to protect submarines from drone attacks at a highly strategic base on the country’s far eastern Kamchatka Peninsula. There are also signs that Russian forces have been taking new steps at a separate base along the Black Sea to shield submarines against uncrewed aerial threats. The appearance of the nets over the submarines at the base in Kamchatka point to how Russia’s concerns about drone threats have extended to critical facilities far removed from the battlefields of Ukraine.

TWZ obtained the imagery showing the netting in place over submarines at the Russian Navy’s base at Rybachiy from Vantor. Business insider was first to report on these images. Rybachiy is notably the homeport for the vast majority of Borei and Borei-A class nuclear ballistic missile submarines, or SSBNs, in service in Russia today. It is also home to various other guided missile and attack submarines assigned to the Russian Navy’s Pacific Fleet.

Images of Rybachiy from Vantor taken on August 4, seen at the top of this story and below, show several different types of submarines fully covered by nets. What is visible in the imagery is broadly consistent with netting that Russian forces have employed in and around Ukraine as a countermeasure against kamikaze drone attacks against assets on the ground and in the water. Similar netting has also observed in use by other armed forces elsewhere globally.

Russian forces at Rybachiy look to have started using these nets back in May based on additional imagery from Vantor. The imagery from May and August show crane barges being used to help erect the nets around submarines at their moorings.

As an aside, floating booms are also seen strung around the piers at Rybachiy. This is something else that is now commonplace at naval bases across Russia, and can help provide an additional barrier to certain threats on or near the surface, particularly explosive-laden kamikaze drone boats.

On Tuesday, the Ministry of Defense in the United Kingdom also published additional imagery from Vantor of the Russian Navy’s base in Novorossiysk along the Black Sea taken back on June 13. The images show several Kilo class attack submarines partially submerged in port. Three of the boats also appear to have anti-drone armor screens installed over their conning towers. A cursory review of additional satellite imagery in Planet Labs’ archive suggests screens were a relatively new additional at that time.

“The Russian Black Sea Fleet has equipped three of its four Kilo class submarines with counter-UAS [uncrewed aerial systems] cages covering the vessels’ conning towers. This was applied as a preventive measure in response to Ukraine’s increased ability to strike targets further from the front line,” according to an accompanying assessment from British authorities earlier this week. “Analysis of commercial satellite imagery dated 13 June 2026 identified that three of the submarines had loosened their moorings and had submerged within the basin. Whilst the majority of the hull was below the surface, their conning towers remained above the waterline, explaining the need for the counter-UAS cage.”

“The fourth submarine, which had not been fitted with a counter-UAS cage, had slipped its mooring lines, manoeuvred away from nearby surface vessels and submerged within the harbour, its conning tower visible above the waterline,” the British government’s assessment continued. “The lack of a counter-UAS cage likely signifies this vessel has been de-prioritised compared to the other three.”

TWZ has also now obtained the June 13 image of Novorossiysk directly from Vantor, as well as another one taken on June 17, which shows the submarines surfaced and at their moorings as usual. This, in turn raises questions about whether or not the boats were submerged in response an attack or indications that one might be imminent. There could be another explanation for why the submarines were temporarily submerged in port, including a force protection readiness exercise in preparation for such an incident.

Growing threats posed by uncrewed aerial systems, as well as uncrewed surface vessels (USV), have already had a marked impact on the establishment of new defensive capabilities and force protection postures at Russian naval and other facilities. This is especially true of sites in more immediate proximity to Ukraine.

Back in 2024, satellite imagery of Novorossiysk notably showed that forces there had painted a silhouette of a submarine and built an actual mock conning tower on a pier at the base. This reflected a broader trend at the time to implement countermeasures against Ukrainian munitions with autonomous image-matching targeting capabilities.

Also in 2024, what looked to be additional overhead protection against drone attacks appeared on the Delta-IV class nuclear ballistic missile submarine Tula at the Russian Navy’s base in Gadzhiyevo in the country’s far northern Murmansk region. What was seen fitted to Tula at that time very rudimentary compared to what has now been seen erected over submarines at Novorossiysk and Rybachiy, which offers far greater and more elaborate coverage . More extensive counter-drone screens have also now appeared on other types of Russian naval vessels.

Ukrainian forces only continue to expand the area, both at sea and on land, that they can hold at risk with uncrewed systems, as well as more traditional missiles. As it stands now, Ukraine uses its ever more diverse arsenal of long-range kamikaze drones and cruise missiles to strike targets across whole swaths of Western Russia, including around the capital Moscow, on a near daily basis.

Ukrainian kamikaze USVs also regularly prowl the Black Sea. Submarines at Novorossiysk, as well as bases on the occupied Crimean Peninsula, have been the wide array of targets struck. There sas another daytime USV attack just yesterday on the Russian-occupied port of Yalta in Crimea. It’s also worth noting here that Ukraine has developed USVs capable of launching kamikaze UAS, combining those two capabilities and creating additional threat vectors Russia’s force have to contend with. In addition, Ukraine now has the ability to hit even moving targets using long-range drones equipped with miniaturized satellite communications terminals. This leaves even ships not sitting static in port very much at risk, which Ukraine has highlighted in recent months as it goes after Russia’s logistics ships in the Sea of Azov, a campaign that is only accelerating and spreading.

As noted, the appearance of the nets at Rybachiy, which sits thousands of miles from Ukraine, speaks to how much further the threat of drone attacks has expanded. This goes beyond long-range strikes, as well. Ukraine’s unprecedented Operation Spiderweb attacks on Russian airbases last year highlighted the dangers posed by near-field attacks launched from deep inside hostile territory closer to their actual targets. Bases in Russia’s far eastern regions were among those targeted in the clandestine operation. Ukrainian forces have also launched attacks on Russian-linked ships in the Mediterranean Sea.

It also worth mentioning here that just this week, a small quadcopter drone equipped with explosive payload was discovered at next to Ukrainian An-124 cargo plane at an airport in Germany. CNN reported today that U.S. authorities have now assessed that uncrewed aerial system to have belonged to a Russian intelligence service. This follows year now of concerning drone incursions over military bases and other critical infrastructure across Western Europe.

Uncrewed aerial threats large and small are not at all limited to the context of the conflict in Ukraine and spillover from it into Europe, either. Drones have been a major factor in the conflict this year with Iran, as well as in other crises in and around the Middle East in recent years.

With the barrier to entry so low, drone threats are only becoming more commonplace globally as they proliferate to increasingly more capable degrees even among smaller nation state armed forces and non-state actors. For the U.S. government, counter-drone defenses for military installations and other critical infrastructure within the homeland, as to protect forces abroad, has become a major priority. Still, American authorities continue to lag in many respects in responding to the serious dangers that very present already.

Altogether, the expansion of counter-drone defenses around submarines at the Russian Navy’s bases at Rybachiy and Novorossiysk reflect very immediate threats emanating from Ukraine, but are also a sign of larger trends globally. Similar force protection measures could well continue to emerge elsewhere, and not just in Russia.

Contact the author: joe@twz.com

articles.title: Pradhan reveals why he quit over Gen Z protest
articles.text: Bhubaneswar: Senior BJP leader and Sambalpur MP Dharmendra Pradhan on Saturday said attempts were made to "mislead" Gen Z during the protests over the NEET paper leak issue, prompting him to quit as Union Education Minister.Pradhan broke his silence on his resignation while addressing students and teachers at GM University here, exactly two weeks after he stepped down amid massive protests at Jantar Mantar in Delhi over the issue."Gen Z is our children. Some people attempted to mislead them. I had no personal issues then. At least two crore children are born in India every year. During the last 10 years, 20 crore children were born. They have aspirations, and they will make India the 'Vishwa Guru'. The post was not important to me," Pradhan said.He said he had approached Prime Minister Narendra Modi and offered to resign from the Union Council of Ministers.Pradhan resigned from the ministry on July 25.At another meeting in Rairakhol, Pradhan hit out at former Odisha chief minister and BJD president Naveen Patnaik, saying he was not disturbed by protests by BJD workers and slogans asking him to "go back".Referring to a protest by BJD youth and student wing activists near the airport, where slogans such as "Dharmendra Pradhan Go Back" were raised, he said, "I am a farmer's son. Even if you tell me to go back, I will come back.""Naveen Babu also calls me a disgrace to the people of Odisha and a bad person," Pradhan said, accusing the BJD president of engaging youths in protests against him."Have I ever done anything that will shame the people of Odisha?" he asked, drawing a loud response of "No" from the gathering."I may not be bringing laurels for the state, but I have never disgraced the people by my work. I will never do any work which will tarnish the state's reputation," he said.Pradhan said he became a Union minister 12 years ago with the blessings of Lord Jagannath and Goddess Samaleswari, the presiding deity of Sambalpur.His remarks against Patnaik came from a dais that was also attended by BJD MLA and deputy leader in the Odisha Assembly Prasanna Acharya."Keeping in view the BJD's protests, I had consulted Prasanna Bhai whether I should go. Prasanna Babu told me to come and assured me that I would be welcomed. I came here after taking his permission," Pradhan said.BJD's Sambalpur district president and former minister Rohit Pujari hit back at Pradhan, saying the BJP leader had been criticised over the handling of the student protests."Nobody had defamed Pradhan. His party and government have defamed him by police resorting to lathi-charge, tear gas and atrocities during the peaceful student agitation at Jantar Mantar. Pradhan was facing criticism because of such incidents. I do not understand why he blames Patnaik for the police excesses on agitating students," Pujari said."Why would Patnaik want to defame him? The whole country knows that 21 children died by suicide because of him. Of the 22 lakh students who appeared for the examination, around 21 lakh students must be under depression. Nobody needs to defame him; he has defamed himself," the BJD leader claimed.Pujari said it was the BJP government's "wrong policy" that had brought a bad name to Pradhan.Meanwhile, sources said Sambalpur police detained around 30 BJD workers as a precautionary measure, anticipating protests by the party's youth and student wings.

articles.title: Project 18 Next Generation Destroyers Still Await Defence Acquisition Council Nod, GRSE Confirms
articles.text:
Garden Reach Shipbuilders and Engineers has confirmed during its latest quarterly earnings call that the Indian Navy’s Project 18 Next Generation Destroyer programme remains in the perspective planning stage and has not yet secured Acceptance of Necessity from the Defence Acquisition Council. The disclosure, made during GRSE’s Q1 concall with analysts and investors, offers one of the clearest official-adjacent timelines yet on where the ambitious warship programme actually stands, cutting through months of speculative reporting about an imminent approval.
What The Perspective Plan Stage Means For P18 Timelines
In India’s defence procurement lifecycle, the perspective plan stage sits well before a programme reaches the Acceptance of Necessity milestone, which is itself the first formal gateway a proposal must clear at the Defence Acquisition Council before moving toward a Request for Proposal and eventual contract negotiation. GRSE’s confirmation that P18 remains at this earlier planning stage indicates that the Navy’s Warship Design Bureau is still finalising core design parameters, propulsion architecture, and weapons fit for the destroyer class rather than working through a Navy-approved requirement document ready for industry-wide tendering. Multiple reports through late 2025 and into 2026 had suggested an AoN could arrive within the current fiscal year, but GRSE’s own management commentary suggests that milestone has not yet been reached even as design work matures.
Why GRSE and MDL Remain Central To The Programme
Garden Reach Shipbuilders and Mazagon Dock Shipbuilders Limited continue to be positioned as the two domestic yards best placed to eventually build the Next Generation Destroyers once the programme clears its approval hurdles. Both shipyards have deep experience building major surface combatants for the Navy, with MDL having delivered the Kolkata and Visakhapatnam class destroyers and GRSE having built a string of corvettes and survey vessels currently in active service. The eventual construction of P18 is expected to proceed under a Strategic Partnership model, which typically involves an Indian shipyard partnering with a foreign original equipment manufacturer to absorb propulsion and combat management system expertise, and industry watchers expect GRSE and MDL to continue contesting for a share of the eventual build once tendering begins.
A Programme Defined By Scale And Ambition
Even with formal approval still pending, Project 18 has already been described by naval planners as India’s most ambitious destroyer programme to date, with an expected displacement exceeding thirteen thousand tonnes that would place it among the largest destroyers ever fielded by the Indian Navy and roughly in the same displacement class as cruiser-tier warships operated by other major navies. The class is envisioned as a successor to the Visakhapatnam class, incorporating extensive automation, an integrated electric propulsion system, and a large vertical launch capacity intended to house a mix of extended-range air defence missiles and long-range strike weapons. Current projections point toward an eventual fleet of ten to twelve vessels built in phases, with an initial batch of four to five ships likely to form the first tranche once contracting begins.
What To Watch Next In The P18 Approval Process
With GRSE’s concall effectively resetting expectations around the programme’s near-term trajectory, the next meaningful milestone to track is Defence Acquisition Council movement on Acceptance of Necessity, which would formally kick off the Request for Proposal process and give industry a concrete requirement document to respond to. Until that approval comes through, P18 remains firmly in the design and planning phase, and any timeline for steel-cutting or contract signing should be treated as provisional. Readers tracking the Indian Navy’s surface combatant modernisation should watch upcoming Defence Acquisition Council meetings and subsequent GRSE and MDL disclosures for the first confirmed signal that the programme has moved past this planning threshold.

articles.title: Netra AEW&C Final Operational Clearance, Clears Path for Mk1A development
articles.text:
The Defence Research and Development Organisation’s (DRDO) Netra Airborne Early Warning and Control (AEW&C) system has achieved Final Operational Clearance (FOC) on June 25, 2026, marking a watershed moment for India’s indigenous airborne surveillance programme. The certification confirms that the EMB-145-based AEW&C platform has successfully completed all developmental and operational evaluations and is now fully cleared for unrestricted operational deployment with the Indian Air Force (IAF).
The FOC represents the culmination of more than a decade of research and development led by DRDO’s Centre for Airborne Systems (CABS). More importantly, it validates India’s ability to design, develop and field an indigenous airborne battle management platform capable of supporting complex air operations without dependence on foreign original equipment manufacturers (OEMs).
Netra serves as one of the IAF’s most important force multipliers, extending the air force’s surveillance horizon far beyond the capabilities of ground-based radar networks. Flying at high altitude, the aircraft continuously monitors large volumes of airspace, detecting and tracking aircraft, cruise missiles and other aerial threats while directing friendly fighter aircraft and coordinating air defence operations.
A key advantage of the FOC-certified system is its contribution to Network-Centric Warfare (NCW). Netra functions as an airborne command-and-control node, integrating airborne sensors, ground-based command centres, air defence networks and fighter aircraft through secure data links. By providing a common operational picture in real time, it enables commanders to make faster decisions and significantly shortens the military Observe-Orient-Decide-Act (OODA) cycle during high-intensity operations.
This capability allows interceptor aircraft to receive target information well before activating their onboard sensors, improving tactical awareness while reducing reaction times against hostile aircraft or missile threats.
The platform also enhances India’s ability to maintain persistent aerial surveillance across sensitive operational sectors. With an endurance of approximately nine hours, extendable through aerial refuelling, Netra can maintain continuous airborne coverage over critical regions, including the Line of Actual Control (LAC), the Line of Control (LoC) and India’s vast maritime approaches.
Such persistent surveillance not only improves early warning but also acts as a strategic deterrent by complicating an adversary’s operational planning. The constant availability of an airborne surveillance platform reduces the possibility of achieving tactical surprise, making it more difficult for hostile forces to conduct covert air operations.
Unlike many indigenous defence programmes that remain largely developmental, Netra has already demonstrated its operational maturity through deployment during real-world military contingencies. The system reportedly supported the Indian Air Force during the Balakot air operations and was again employed during Operation Sindoor in 2025, providing airborne surveillance, battle management and situational awareness in high-threat operational environments.
These deployments validated the performance of the aircraft’s indigenous Active Electronically Scanned Array (AESA) radar, Electronic Support Measures (ESM) and mission management systems under actual operational conditions, reinforcing confidence in the platform’s reliability.
Perhaps the most strategically significant aspect of the Netra programme is its sovereign software architecture. Since the system has been developed domestically, India retains complete control over its mission software, operational algorithms and future upgrades. Unlike imported airborne early warning platforms, which often require OEM support for software modifications or capability enhancements, Netra can be adapted to emerging threats entirely within the country.
This flexibility enables DRDO and the IAF to rapidly integrate new threat libraries, improve sensor fusion algorithms and introduce additional operational capabilities without external approvals or technology restrictions.
The successful completion of the current programme also lays the foundation for the much more capable Netra Mk2. While the existing AEW&C fleet operates from the Embraer EMB-145 regional jet and provides approximately 240-degree radar coverage, the next-generation system will transition to the significantly larger Airbus A321 platform.
The increased size and payload capacity of the A321 will allow the installation of a more powerful radar, greater electrical power generation, additional operator consoles and increased fuel capacity. The Netra Mk2 is expected to deliver radar detection ranges exceeding 500 kilometres while offering near-360-degree surveillance coverage, eliminating the blind sectors associated with the current configuration.
Beyond its operational capabilities, the Netra programme has become a model for India’s Atmanirbhar Bharat initiative. The project demonstrates how sustained collaboration between DRDO, the Indian Air Force, public-sector enterprises and private industry can deliver strategically important defence systems that meet operational requirements while reducing dependence on imported technologies.

articles.title: Japan May Deploy F-2 Fighters to India for First Bilateral Exercise, Signalling Deeper Indo-Pacific Air Cooperation
articles.text:
Japan is reportedly preparing to deploy its Mitsubishi F-2 fighter aircraft to India for the first time for a bilateral air exercise later this month, a move that would mark a significant expansion of air-power cooperation between New Delhi and Tokyo. The reported deployment comes as Japanese Defence Minister Shinjiro Koizumi prepares for a visit to India and Australia beginning August 17, with discussions on defence cooperation expected to form a major part of his engagement in New Delhi.
According to Chinese state media outlet Global Times, Japanese officials have indicated that Tokyo views the proposed fighter deployment in the context of the broader strategic competition with China. The report portrayed the exercise as part of Japan’s effort to strengthen military coordination with India. However, the Chinese interpretation should be separated from the operational significance of the exercise itself. India and Japan have been steadily expanding defence cooperation for several years, including increasingly sophisticated air, maritime and land exercises.
There is an important correction to some descriptions of the development. A Japanese F-2 deployment to India would be the first time Japanese F-2 fighters operate from Indian territory for a bilateral fighter exercise, but it would not be the first time the F-2 has participated in an India-Japan fighter exercise. During Veer Guardian 2023, Japan deployed four F-2 fighters and four F-15 fighters to Hyakuri Air Base, where they trained against four Indian Air Force Su-30MKIs. India’s Ministry of Defence described that event as the first bilateral fighter aircraft exercise between the two countries.
The potential reversal of the deployment direction is therefore strategically interesting. In 2023, Indian fighters travelled to Japan to train against Japanese aircraft. If the reported 2026 exercise goes ahead with F-2s operating from India, Japanese pilots would instead gain experience operating from Indian bases and within India’s airspace environment. Such an arrangement can provide valuable practical exposure to different operating procedures, airspace management systems, logistics arrangements and climatic conditions.
The F-2 itself is particularly relevant for such training because it is a Japanese-developed multirole fighter derived from the F-16 design but substantially modified for Japanese requirements. The aircraft incorporates a larger wing, Japanese-developed avionics and an indigenous active electronically scanned array radar, giving it a different sensor and weapons architecture from conventional F-16 variants.
For the Indian Air Force, interaction with the F-2 could provide another useful opportunity for dissimilar air-combat training. India operates a diverse fighter fleet comprising Russian-origin Su-30MKIs, French Rafales and Mirage 2000s, indigenous Tejas fighters and other platforms. Training against aircraft with different radar characteristics, electronic warfare systems, flight-control philosophies and tactical doctrines can help improve pilot preparedness for complex air operations.
The timing also fits into a broader expansion of India-Japan defence cooperation. The two countries have progressively increased military exercises and defence-industrial engagement, while both are members of the Quad alongside the United States and Australia. Japan’s Ministry of Defence records multiple bilateral exercises with India, while Japanese and Indian forces have also expanded cooperation across maritime and ground domains.
China’s reaction is therefore unsurprising, particularly given the increasingly competitive security environment in the Indo-Pacific. Global Times framed the proposed F-2 deployment as part of Tokyo’s effort to counter China and deepen military coordination with New Delhi. Chinese analysts have also questioned whether Japan’s expanding overseas defence cooperation represents a broader transformation of its post-war security posture.
For India, however, the exercise need not be viewed exclusively through an anti-China lens. New Delhi has consistently pursued strategic autonomy while simultaneously expanding military partnerships with countries that can contribute to its operational capabilities. Exercises with Japan can improve interoperability and provide exposure to another advanced air force without creating a formal military alliance.

articles.title: American Space Watchers Stunned as Indian Startup Astrobase Unveils 80-Tonne-Class FFSC Rocket Engine in Bengaluru
articles.text:
India’s rapidly expanding private space sector has unveiled a rocket propulsion system that is attracting international attention, with Bengaluru-based Astrobase Space Technologies revealing its Everest engine, an 800-kilonewton-class liquid oxygen-methane Full-Flow Staged Combustion (FFSC) rocket engine. The company describes it as India’s first privately developed FFSC engine, placing an Indian startup in pursuit of one of the most technically demanding propulsion architectures in modern rocketry.
The engine, equivalent to roughly an 80-tonne thrust class system, was unveiled on August 7 as a fully integrated engine designed and manufactured in Bengaluru. The development has generated significant interest among international space observers because FFSC technology remains exceptionally challenging, with SpaceX’s Raptor being the best-known operational example. Astrobase’s achievement is particularly notable because the company was founded only in 2024.
Astrobase’s Everest uses liquid oxygen and methane, commonly referred to as a methalox propulsion system. The company says the engine is designed to produce approximately 800 kN of vacuum thrust, with a throttle range that allows substantial variation in thrust. India’s space regulator, IN-SPACe, had earlier identified Astrobase’s 800 kN LOX-methane FFSC engine as a privately developed propulsion technology intended for reusable launch systems.
What makes the engine particularly significant is its combustion cycle. In a conventional rocket engine, some propellant can be diverted to drive turbopumps, with the resulting gas eventually discarded or used in a less efficient manner. An FFSC architecture instead routes both the fuel-rich and oxidizer-rich flows through separate preburners and turbomachinery before sending them into the main combustion chamber. In principle, this allows the engine to operate at very high chamber pressures while extracting more energy from the propellant.
That efficiency is particularly valuable for reusable launch vehicles. Higher propulsion efficiency can translate into greater payload capability, improved mass fractions and more flexibility in reserving propellant for controlled first-stage recovery. The methane fuel also offers characteristics attractive for reusable systems, including relatively clean combustion compared with kerosene-based propulsion.
The technological challenge, however, is enormous. FFSC engines require extremely demanding turbomachinery, combustion control, seals, bearings, injectors, cooling systems and materials capable of surviving highly energetic environments. The oxygen-rich side of the cycle is especially demanding because hot, high-pressure oxygen can be extremely aggressive toward conventional materials.
Astrobase has been building the supporting industrial ecosystem alongside the engine. The company operates a 46,000-square-foot manufacturing and integration facility in Bengaluru, while its high-thrust engine testing infrastructure is located near Anantapur in Andhra Pradesh. The private test facility is designed around a stand capable of handling substantially more thrust than the 800 kN engine’s nominal output.
The company’s manufacturing strategy also makes extensive use of additive manufacturing. Astrobase previously announced the arrival of what it described as India’s largest industrial 3D printer, intended to manufacture complex components for its FFSC engines. Additive manufacturing can reduce part count, simplify intricate internal passages and accelerate iteration during development, although flight qualification and long-duration reliability remain major challenges.
The unveiling should nevertheless be viewed as a development milestone rather than proof of a flight-ready engine. Astrobase has previously reported successful subscale hot-fire testing and turbopump testing, but the full-scale Everest engine still needs to demonstrate sustained hot-fire performance before its ultimate capability can be judged. The company plans to conduct full-scale testing at its Andhra Pradesh facility.
The potential payoff is substantial. Astrobase is developing a reusable orbital launch vehicle around its propulsion technology and has outlined a vehicle capable of carrying several tonnes to low Earth orbit. Its IN-SPACe documentation describes a planned reusable two-stage architecture targeting approximately 4.2 tonnes to a 500-kilometre orbit.
For India, the importance of Everest extends beyond a single startup or engine. Indigenous mastery of high-performance methalox propulsion could become an important building block for reusable launch vehicles, larger orbital rockets and eventually more ambitious commercial space systems. It also demonstrates how India’s private space reforms are beginning to move beyond satellite manufacturing and small launch vehicles into some of the most difficult areas of aerospace engineering.

articles.title: Should India Develop Its Own Sixth-Generation Fighter Alongside Global Partnerships?
articles.text:
India’s reported interest in participating in an international sixth-generation fighter programme has opened an important debate about the future of the Indian Air Force (IAF). With New Delhi evaluating potential collaboration with Europe’s Future Combat Air System (FCAS) and the UK-Italy-Japan-led Global Combat Air Programme (GCAP), defence planners face a fundamental question: should India rely on international partnerships for its next-generation combat aircraft, or should it simultaneously develop its own indigenous sixth-generation platform?
A related question has also emerged. As China advances programmes believed to include large stealth aircraft and long-range strike platforms, should India consider developing a strategic bomber comparable to China’s reported “J-36”-type concepts?
The answers point toward a dual-track strategy centred on indigenous capability while leveraging international cooperation to accelerate technological development.
The strongest argument for joining a global sixth-generation programme is not the aircraft itself but the technologies that accompany it.
Sixth-generation fighters are expected to incorporate artificial intelligence-assisted mission management, adaptive engines, advanced stealth materials, sensor fusion, collaborative combat aircraft, quantum-resistant communications and highly networked “combat cloud” architectures.
Developing every one of these technologies independently would require enormous investments over several decades.
Participation in an international programme offers India an opportunity to work alongside some of the world’s most advanced aerospace industries while exposing Indian engineers and manufacturers to cutting-edge technologies that would otherwise take years to develop domestically.
However, international cooperation should not replace indigenous development.
India’s experience with previous imported platforms has consistently demonstrated the importance of technological sovereignty. Access restrictions, proprietary software, export controls and dependence on foreign suppliers have often complicated weapon integration, upgrades and lifecycle management.
A future indigenous sixth-generation fighter would allow India to maintain complete control over mission software, weapons integration, electronic warfare systems and future upgrades without requiring approval from external partners.
This autonomy has become increasingly important as modern combat aircraft evolve into software-defined platforms.
The Advanced Medium Combat Aircraft (AMCA) illustrates this philosophy.
Although India continues to seek international assistance in critical areas such as propulsion and advanced materials, the AMCA remains fundamentally an indigenous programme designed to provide the Indian Air Force with long-term strategic independence.
A similar model could shape India’s sixth-generation ambitions.
Rather than choosing between international collaboration and domestic development, New Delhi could pursue both simultaneously.
Participation in programmes such as FCAS or GCAP would expose Indian industry to emerging technologies, while those technologies could subsequently influence future indigenous programmes.
This process of technological cross-pollination has historically benefited aerospace industries worldwide.
Many countries participating in multinational aircraft programmes have successfully transferred expertise into their own national aerospace capabilities, accelerating domestic innovation without abandoning sovereign design ambitions.
Industrial development is another major consideration.
India’s aerospace ecosystem is expanding rapidly through public and private participation in programmes involving fighters, missiles, radars, unmanned systems and advanced manufacturing.
Meaningful participation in a sixth-generation programme would integrate Indian companies into long-term global supply chains involving composite materials, digital engineering, avionics, artificial intelligence and advanced propulsion.
Such industrial participation could strengthen India’s defence manufacturing sector well beyond combat aircraft alone.
The debate becomes more complex when discussing strategic bombers.
China’s reported development of large stealth aircraft has naturally generated speculation about whether India should pursue a similar capability.
On paper, a strategic bomber offers significant advantages.
It can carry large payloads over intercontinental distances, remain airborne for extended periods and launch long-range cruise missiles far from hostile airspace.
For major powers with global military commitments, strategic bombers remain an important component of power projection.
India’s strategic requirements, however, differ substantially.
The Indian Air Force’s immediate priority remains rebuilding fighter squadron strength while inducting Tejas Mk1A, developing the Tejas Mk2, operationalising the AMCA and modernising existing Su-30MKI and Rafale fleets.
These programmes already demand significant financial and industrial resources.
Launching an entirely new strategic bomber programme would require additional investments measured in tens of billions of dollars, along with decades of research into large stealth airframes, high-thrust engines, specialised avionics and long-range weapons integration.
Operational doctrine also favours alternative approaches.
Modern stand-off weapons have fundamentally changed long-range strike operations.
Aircraft such as the Rafale, Su-30MKI and future AMCA variants can already deliver precision-guided cruise missiles hundreds of kilometres from their targets while remaining outside the engagement envelope of many air defence systems.
Long-range air-launched cruise missiles, hypersonic weapons and aerial refuelling increasingly allow multirole fighters to perform missions that once required dedicated strategic bombers.
India’s evolving missile inventory further reduces the necessity for a bomber fleet.
The country’s nuclear deterrent increasingly rests on a robust triad comprising land-based Agni ballistic missiles, Arihant-class nuclear-powered ballistic missile submarines and air-delivered nuclear capabilities.
Among these, ballistic missile submarines provide the most survivable second-strike capability because they remain concealed beneath the ocean.
From a strategic deterrence perspective, expanding the sea-based nuclear deterrent often delivers greater survivability than investing in vulnerable airborne bomber fleets.
This does not mean India should completely dismiss long-range strike aviation.
Future sixth-generation aircraft may possess significantly greater range, payload and endurance than today’s fighters while controlling multiple autonomous combat drones carrying additional weapons.
Such systems could achieve many of the operational effects traditionally associated with bombers without requiring a separate class of very large aircraft.
Collaborative combat aircraft, often referred to as loyal wingmen, may further expand strike capacity by accompanying crewed fighters into contested airspace while carrying sensors, electronic warfare equipment or precision munitions.
Consequently, the distinction between heavy fighter and strategic bomber may become increasingly blurred during the coming decades.
For India, the more practical objective may be developing an extended-range sixth-generation combat aircraft capable of operating across the Indian Ocean and Indo-Pacific while integrating seamlessly with unmanned systems, space-based assets and advanced long-range weapons.
Such an approach would deliver strategic reach without the enormous financial burden associated with building a dedicated stealth bomber fleet.
Ultimately, India’s long-term air power strategy should rest on three complementary pillars. International collaboration can accelerate access to critical technologies, indigenous programmes such as the AMCA can preserve strategic autonomy, and continued investment in missiles, drones and network-centric warfare can provide long-range strike capability without diverting resources toward a costly strategic bomber programme.

articles.title: BrahMos Can’t Do It All: Why India Needs a High-Volume 500-km Subsonic Cruise Missile
articles.text:
India’s missile arsenal has evolved rapidly over the past decade, with systems such as the supersonic BrahMos and the upcoming Long-Range Land Attack Cruise Missile (LR-LACM) providing the armed forces with formidable long-range precision strike capabilities. However, as modern conflicts increasingly demonstrate the importance of sustained, high-volume precision fires, a capability gap is becoming apparent. Between short-range tactical weapons and high-end strategic cruise missiles lies an operational requirement for a mass-produced, cost-effective subsonic cruise missile with a range of around 500 km.
Such a missile would not compete with BrahMos or the LR-LACM. Instead, it would complement them by addressing missions where cost, production volume and operational flexibility are more important than maximum speed or strategic reach.
One of the strongest arguments for developing such a weapon lies in the economics of modern missile warfare. BrahMos is among the world’s most capable supersonic cruise missiles, combining high speed, precision and survivability. Those capabilities, however, come at a significant manufacturing cost due to its ramjet propulsion system, advanced seeker technologies and sophisticated guidance architecture. Similarly, the LR-LACM is being developed primarily as a strategic deep-strike asset capable of engaging high-value targets at extended ranges.
During an extended conflict, relying exclusively on these premium systems for every strike mission would quickly become unsustainable. Many battlefield targets—including logistics hubs, ammunition depots, radar installations, bridges, fuel storage facilities and secondary command centres—do not necessarily require the speed and sophistication of a BrahMos. Employing an expensive strategic missile against relatively lower-value tactical targets risks depleting limited inventories while imposing a heavy financial burden.
A simpler subsonic cruise missile capable of striking targets up to 500 km away could deliver the required operational effect at a fraction of the cost, allowing India’s strategic missile stockpiles to be preserved for the missions they were specifically designed to perform.
Production capacity presents another compelling reason for such a programme. High-performance cruise missiles depend on specialised manufacturing infrastructure, complex propulsion systems, precision electronics and tightly controlled supply chains. Scaling production rapidly during wartime is extremely difficult because many critical components require long manufacturing lead times and highly specialised industrial processes.
A lower-cost missile designed from the outset for mass production could alleviate these constraints. By using simplified designs, modular construction techniques and greater participation from India’s growing private defence sector, production could be distributed across multiple industrial facilities rather than relying solely on existing strategic missile production lines. Emerging indigenous compact turbofan programmes, including modular engines in the 4.5 kN thrust class being developed by private industry, could eventually provide an indigenous propulsion solution that further strengthens production resilience.
Perhaps the greatest operational advantage of a mass-produced subsonic cruise missile lies in its ability to overwhelm enemy air defences. Modern integrated air defence systems (IADS) possess sophisticated radars and interceptors capable of engaging multiple incoming threats, but they remain constrained by the finite number and high cost of interceptor missiles.
Launching large salvos of relatively inexpensive cruise missiles forces defenders into difficult decisions. Even if a significant proportion of the attacking missiles are intercepted, defenders expend valuable and costly surface-to-air missiles in the process. This creates an asymmetric cost exchange in which the attacker imposes disproportionate economic pressure while gradually reducing the defender’s interceptor inventory.
Once air defence networks have been saturated or partially depleted, more valuable assets—including BrahMos, LR-LACM or air-launched stand-off weapons—can exploit the resulting gaps to engage high-priority targets with a greater probability of success. Rather than replacing premium weapons, a mass-produced cruise missile would serve as an important force multiplier within a layered strike campaign.
Another important consideration is command flexibility. Strategic missiles are typically controlled at higher operational and political levels because of their limited numbers, strategic implications and high replacement cost. Tactical commanders may therefore have limited access to these assets during rapidly evolving battlefield situations.
A widely available 500-km subsonic cruise missile would provide theatre commanders with an organic precision-strike capability capable of engaging enemy airfields, logistics hubs, troop concentration areas, fuel depots and command facilities across operational theatres without requiring the allocation of scarce strategic assets. Such flexibility would significantly improve responsiveness during high-tempo operations.
Developing such a capability also aligns with the broader transformation of India’s defence industrial ecosystem. The increasing participation of private companies in propulsion systems, guidance technologies, composite manufacturing and autonomous flight systems creates an opportunity to build parallel production capacity outside traditional government-led programmes. This diversified industrial base would enhance resilience during crises while accelerating production when demand increases.
The objective, therefore, is not to replace existing missile systems but to create a more balanced strike portfolio. BrahMos would remain the preferred weapon for time-sensitive, heavily defended and high-value targets requiring speed and kinetic impact. The LR-LACM would continue to provide strategic deep-strike capability against critical infrastructure and command networks far inside hostile territory. A 500-km subsonic cruise missile would occupy the tier below them, delivering affordable precision strike capability in large numbers against tactical and operational targets.
Modern conflicts have repeatedly shown that victory is determined not only by possessing technologically superior weapons but also by sustaining precision fires over extended periods. Quantity, affordability and production capacity have become as important as individual weapon performance. By introducing a high-volume subsonic cruise missile into its inventory, India would add a crucial layer to its strike capability—one that preserves elite strategic weapons for decisive missions while providing commanders with the mass, flexibility and affordability needed for prolonged, high-intensity warfare.

articles.title: Agni-IV “0077” OR ” 11″ Mystery: Does the Marking Reveal India Has 77 Missiles? My Analysis of the SFC Test
articles.text:
The marking visible on the Agni-IV tested by India’s Strategic Forces Command has triggered an interesting debate in Indian defence circles. Some observers initially read the number as “0077” and suggested that it could indicate the 77th missile of the series, potentially implying that India has at least 77 Agni-IV missiles. Others have argued that the marking is actually “0011”, while another interpretation circulating online suggests that the number could be a much longer serial or production identification code.
After examining the supplied photograph closely, my assessment is that the visible marking should not be used to estimate India’s Agni-IV inventory. More importantly, the image does appear to show Arabic/Latin numerals, not Devanagari numerals. The number is visually much closer to 0077 than to the Devanagari representation ००७७ or the alternative ४००११ suggested in the discussion. However, the photograph’s resolution and distortion make the characters immediately before the digits difficult to establish with absolute certainty.
The distinction is important because a serial number does not necessarily equal the total number of missiles manufactured or held in inventory. Defence production systems routinely use identification numbers associated with individual vehicles, production lots, test articles, stages, components or other manufacturing records. A missile carrying “0077” could therefore be the 77th item in a particular numbering sequence without meaning that exactly 76 identical operational missiles preceded it.
The fact that the latest launch was conducted under the aegis of the Strategic Forces Command adds another interesting dimension. The Ministry of Defence confirmed that the August 6 Agni-IV launch validated operational and technical parameters and was conducted under SFC. That makes it reasonable to describe the event as an operational/user trial, rather than simply another DRDO development test.
But even that does not allow us to conclude that the missile photographed was necessarily drawn from a specific operational stockpile. Strategic missile user trials can involve production-standard or operationally representative missiles, and the exact relationship between the test article and the deployable inventory is not publicly disclosed.
There is another reason to be cautious about the “77 missiles” theory. The Agni-IV has undergone a relatively limited number of publicly acknowledged flight tests compared with the proposed inventory figure. The recent launch has been described by The Times of India as the 10th Agni-IV test overall and the sixth conducted by the Strategic Forces Command. Therefore, “0077” clearly cannot simply be interpreted as “the 77th publicly tested Agni-IV.”
The more plausible explanation is that the marking represents an internal serial, manufacturing identification, configuration number or other traceability code. Such markings are valuable to the manufacturer and military because individual systems need to be tracked throughout production, acceptance, maintenance and operational life. Without access to India’s missile production documentation, assigning a specific meaning to the number would be speculation.
The Devanagari argument can also be settled fairly easily from the photograph. The missile carries Hindi/Devanagari text, including “अग्नि”, but the numeric marking immediately underneath appears to use Arabic numerals. If it were “40011” written in Devanagari, one would expect the characters ४००११, which are visually different from what is visible in the photograph. The image therefore does not provide strong evidence for the “40011” interpretation.
My confidence level would therefore be: the marking probably contains “0077”, but its meaning is unknown; it does not establish an inventory of 77 Agni-IV missiles. The SFC involvement does strengthen the case that this was an operationally relevant missile, but it does not reveal the size of India’s stockpile.

articles.title: Pakistan Defence Minister Khawaja Asif Calls for ‘Muslim NATO’ to Target India and Israel
articles.text:
Recent high-level statements from Islamabad have reignited intense geopolitical debates across South Asia and the Middle East, following remarks by Pakistan’s Defence Minister Khawaja Asif advocating for the creation of a collective military alliance among Muslim-majority nations. Labelled by commentators and proponents as a Muslim or Islamic NATO, the proposed security framework seeks to unite key regional players into a consolidated front. Within domestic and regional parliamentary discussions, senior Pakistani leadership has increasingly framed such an alliance around a shared posture directed against traditional regional adversaries, explicitly naming both India and Israel as primary focal points of concern.
The push for a pan-Islamic military coalition comes amid escalating volatility across West Asia and persistent strategic friction in South Asia. Proponents of the concept within Pakistan argue that existing bilateral defense agreements—such as those linking Islamabad with key Gulf states like Saudi Arabia—should be expanded to incorporate powerhouses like Turkey and Qatar into a unified command or mutual defense architecture. By pooling military resources, intelligence, and defense industrial capabilities, proponents claim the bloc would give the Muslim world a stronger deterrent voice against external interventions and perceived aggressions. However, critics and strategic analysts point out that deep-seated rivalries, divergent foreign policies, and competing leadership ambitions among potential member states have historically rendered such ambitious coalitions virtually unworkable.
For New Delhi, any institutionalized security mechanism spearheaded by Pakistan that identifies India as a primary adversary demands continuous strategic vigilance. Indian security planners have long monitored Islamabad’s attempts to mobilize international Islamic platforms to advance bilateral disputes, particularly regarding Kashmir and cross-border issues. While India has successfully cultivated robust, independent strategic and economic partnerships with major Middle Eastern nations over the past decade—effectively delinking bilateral ties from regional friction points—a formalized ideological military bloc introduces fresh diplomatic variables. New Delhi’s rising economic weight and role as a net security provider in the broader region ensure that key international partners remain committed to pragmatism rather than ideological posturing, yet the rhetoric from Islamabad underscores the persistent complexities of India’s immediate security environment.

articles.title: DeepMind’s hurricane breakthrough has surprised weather scientists
articles.text:
In October 2025, a storm brewed over the Caribbean Sea. Weather models differed on its trajectory. Would it remain weak and end up in Haiti, or would it intensify and head to Jamaica? Artificial intelligence model WeatherNext, developed by Google’s DeepMind and Google Research, went with the latter. Five days before landfall, it predicted with 80 percent confidence that the storm system would hit Jamaica as a Category 5 hurricane.

Hurricane Melissa was catastrophic, causing flooding and landslides across Jamaica. But the AI model helped forecasters give an earlier warning to communities in its path, so they could better prepare.

In a paper published on Thursday in Nature, researchers show that the WeatherNext AI model can predict cyclones with unprecedented accuracy. On average, it gives forecasters a day more lead time than existing models; this means its predictions three days out are as accurate as previous models’ predictions two days out. On the ground, that extra day can mean a lot.

articles.title: Show HN: Wyzer Programming Language
articles.text:
So i've been working on this project since a few days (or months i should say), it's called wyzer (meaning wiser) it's a statically typed, compiled, resource-oriented programming language with integrated distributed safety via choreographic programming and perceus memory model, The reason why i began this project is out of frustration from Rust, you see it does provide safety for your memory by the strict type checking but what it does not gurantee safety against are distributed deadlocks which is basically a few independent nodes or services wait permanently for resources or messages held by each other, forming a circular wait, the rest are cross-service correctness and protocol mismatch as well. If we are specific over here Wyzer works on mainly generalizing the concept of choreographic programming in a high level programming language because its the very few attempts of actually solving these gaps of safety. Instead of borrow checkers and lifetimes wyzer has linear/affine types and a perceus reference counting which is computationally much simpler for an LSP to understand as well

after 5 months of research and a few weeks of development i am soon going to release version 0.1.0 of it, if you would like to contribute to it you're most welcome!
